Today Freya Axelsen had every chance of setting a new record. Right now three hundred and fifty thousand people were watching her stream, and the number was climbing fast, because the broadcast was moving on to the Q&A.

If the live audience hit four hundred thousand, it would be the all-time world record for the entire coaching industry.

No one had ever managed it before her. Even the famous and obscenely rich Tony Bobbins, in his prime, had only pulled three hundred and ninety thousand, and that was after decades in the market and with a face the whole world knew! Now Freya had a shot at smashing that ceiling with room to spare and securing her fame for years to come. And if anyone thought it was just dumb luck, Freya knew better: fortune smiles only on prepared minds and hands ready to act.

At first things had gone merely okay. The first hour was a lecture on how to achieve your goals. It was the most enjoyable part, but only a hundred thousand showed up. Expected, but not Freya's level, not with her four million on Instagram and another twelve on TikTok. Freya didn't care for TikTok; it lacked a serious audience, but the algorithms had decided otherwise.

Another hour went to questions along the lines of "the best age to start a startup" and "how to get up and get going," which followers had submitted through a form before the stream. The questions went down well and pushed the live count up to two hundred thousand.

But it still wasn't enough. It was a plateau. Two hundred thousand was a plateau that got harder to break through every time.

And that was when Freya went all in, as the New York hustlers liked to say. In twenty minutes, right in the middle of the stream, her assistants bolted on a payment form and wrote posts for social media. And the surprise segment of the broadcast began: open questions for donations. No moderation, but on Freya's terms.
